strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important limitation of existing multi-token prediction (MTP) methods: their restriction to short-horizon future token dependencies due to the scalability limits of adding auxiliary heads.

The proposed Future Summary Prediction (FSP) framework is conceptually clean and elegant, requiring only a single auxiliary head regardless of future horizon length, in contrast to MTP variants that need one head per future position.

The synthetic task analysis (path-star graph and modified sibling discovery) is a strong contribution in its own right: it clearly illustrates why long-range supervision matters (path-star) and why adaptive/learned summaries are needed over indiscriminate handcrafted summaries (sibling discovery), providing good mechanistic intuition before scaling up.

Large-scale pretraining experiments at 3B and 1T-token 8B scale are rare in this line of work due to compute cost, and the paper's willingness to run six method variants at this scale (Table 3) adds credibility and thoroughness that many papers in this area lack.
Reasonably thorough ablations are provided (tf-idf reweighting on/off, different summary window sizes τ, RevLM layer depth for extracting the summary embedding), which helps clarify design choices.

The related work section clearly differentiates FSP from prior bidirectional/reverse-model approaches (BST, MiM) and prior MTP variants (DeepSeek-MTP, TRELAWNEY, register tokens), correctly identifying conceptual novelty.
weaknesses: Results are mixed and somewhat inconsistent with the paper's central claims: at 3B scale, DeepSeek-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on most tasks (ARC-Easy/Challenge, MBPP, HumanEval+), with FSP only winning on math reasoning, undercutting the narrative of consistent superiority.
At 8B scale, NTP still outperforms FSP-RevLM on GSM8K, which is one of the flagship 'long-horizon reasoning' benchmarks the paper emphasizes, weakening the core motivating claim.

The claim that 'FSP-RevLM scales more favorably than DS-MTP' from 3B to 8B is based on only two model sizes/data points, which is weak evidence for a scaling trend and should be tempered or better substantiated (e.g., with an intermediate scale).

The extra compute cost of training a full reverse language model (comparable size to the forward model, trained on the same large corpus) is dismissed via a distillation analogy as 'amortized,' but this substantially increases total training compute versus NTP/MTP/DS-MTP baselines; the paper does not report or discuss this overhead quantitatively, making practical cost-benefit comparisons difficult.

Table 3's ablation deliberately excludes DS-MTP as a comparison point (justified by architectural differences), but DS-MTP is shown elsewhere to be a strong baseline, so its absence from the core auxiliary-target analysis leaves a gap in understanding whether FSP's gains would hold against the strongest baseline under matched conditions.

MTP and DS-MTP baselines are restricted to a single auxiliary head throughout, which is a nonstandard and potentially disadvantageous configuration for these baselines relative to how they are typically deployed in production systems (e.g., DeepSeek-V3 uses more), raising concerns about whether comparisons are fully fair.

Reported standard errors for ARC accuracy are exactly 0.000 in multiple cases despite claiming results over 3 random seeds, which is suspicious and raises questions about whether variance was properly measured or reported for that metric.

No qualitative analysis or example generations are provided to substantiate claims about improved long-horizon reasoning, planning, or creative writing (the pass@k diversity plots are the only qualitative-adjacent evidence, and only for math tasks).

The abstract and intro emphasize 'gains of up to 5%,' which appears to selectively highlight the most favorable comparisons while the full results tables show a more mixed picture, giving an overclaiming impression relative to the actual evidence.

strengths: The core idea of predicting a compact 'future summary' rather than individual future tokens is a reasonable and relatively novel extension of MTP, addressing a real limitation (short horizon of MTP).
Two clearly articulated variants (handcrafted bag-of-words/BCE and learned RevLM-based summary) give a nice spectrum from interpretable to more powerful supervision.

The synthetic diagnostic experiments (path-star graph, modified sibling discovery) are a nice mechanistic complement to the large-scale results, illustrating in a controlled setting why long-range and adaptive summaries can help avoid shortcut learning/gradient starvation.

Large-scale pretraining experiments at 3B and 8B parameters with 250B/1T tokens are computationally substantial and rare in the literature, and the paper includes a reasonably broad set of baselines (NTP, MTP, DS-MTP, MTP-Skip, FSP-BCE with different windows) plus some ablations (tf-idf reweighting, RevLM layer depth).
The paper is clearly written and the architecture/objective formalism (Section 2) is precise and easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central efficiency/compute claim is questionable: FSP-RevLM requires training an entire additional reverse language model on the full pretraining corpus, which is comparable in cost to training a second forward model, yet the paper explicitly excludes this cost from the reported comparisons under an 'iso-data, not iso-compute' justification. This makes the core comparison to NTP/MTP/DS-MTP potentially unfair, since none of those baselines receive an equivalent extra compute budget (e.g., a longer-trained or larger NTP baseline is never tested as a compute-matched control).

Results are inconsistent and do not robustly support the paper's central claims: at 3B scale, DeepSeek-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on most benchmarks (MBPP, HumanEval+, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge), and at 8B scale NTP still beats FSP-RevLM on GSM8K. The claim that FSP-RevLM 'scales more favorably' rests on only two model sizes (3B, 8B), which is weak evidence for a genuine scaling trend.

Several reported standard errors for ARC-Easy/ARC-Challenge are exactly 0.000 despite averaging over 3 seeds, which is suspicious and raises concerns about the evaluation protocol (e.g., possibly deterministic/greedy decoding making the seed variation meaningless), undermining confidence in the statistical rigor of the comparisons.

The restriction of MTP and DS-MTP to a single auxiliary head diverges from how these methods are used in practice (e.g., DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-3 use multiple auxiliary heads), so the comparison, while internally consistent, may not reflect the true competitive baseline performance achievable by MTP-style methods in production settings.

The magnitude of gains highlighted in the abstract/intro ('up to 5% on math and coding') is somewhat selectively reported; many benchmarks show ties or losses to baselines (e.g., HumanEval+ ties with MTP at 8B, GSM8K underperforms NTP at 8B), and the overall picture is more mixed than the framing suggests.

The synthetic experiments use tiny GPT-Mini models (12 layers, 384 dim) that may not transfer cleanly to the qualitative claims made about 8B-scale behavior; the paper asserts this transfer largely through narrative rather than direct empirical linkage.

Missing simpler ablations that would isolate the source of FSP-RevLM's benefit, e.g., a continuous but non-RevLM learned summary (such as a simple pooled embedding of future tokens or a smaller/no separate teacher model), to disentangle the benefit of 'learned summary' from the extra compute/parameters invested in training a full auxiliary reverse LM.

No discussion of additional latency/memory overhead from training and periodically loading the RevLM as a teacher, nor a systematic cost-benefit analysis to establish whether the (already modest and inconsistent) accuracy gains justify roughly doubling the pretraining pipeline complexity and compute.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: replacing per-token auxiliary heads (MTP) with a single head that predicts a compact summary of the long-term future, addressing the scalability limitation of MTP-style methods in a principled way.

Two complementary summary construction strategies (handcrafted bag-of-words BCE summary and learned RevLM-distilled summary) are clearly motivated and their trade-offs (noise from irrelevant future tokens vs. adaptive filtering) are cleanly illustrated.

The synthetic analyses (path-star graph and modified sibling discovery) are well-designed diagnostic experiments that isolate and clearly demonstrate the mechanism by which FSP reduces teacher forcing and outperforms MTP/NTP, with intuitive visualizations.

Large-scale pretraining experiments at both 3B (250B tokens) and 8B (1T tokens) scale are a significant and costly undertaking, and the breadth of baselines compared (NTP, MTP, DeepSeek-MTP, MTP-Skip, FSP-BCE at multiple window sizes, FSP-RevLM) is unusually thorough for this kind of study.
Extensive ablations (tf-idf reweighting, RevLM layer depth, window size tau) at both scales strengthen the empirical grounding of design choices.
Clear positioning relative to prior bidirectional/reverse-model work (BST, Meet-in-the-Middle) and MTP variants (DeepSeek-MTP, TRELAWNEY, L-MTP, register tokens).
weaknesses: Real-world results are mixed and do not consistently support the paper's central claim: at 3B scale, DeepSeek-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on most tasks (ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MBPP, HumanEval+), with FSP-RevLM winning only on math reasoning; this considerably weakens the generality of the proposed method's advantage.

The DS-MTP baseline behaves oddly at 8B scale (e.g., ARC-Easy 61.7% vs. NTP's 71.8%, a large regression), which is suspicious and raises concerns about whether DS-MTP was properly tuned/implemented, undermining confidence in the comparison used to argue FSP-RevLM's superiority.

On GSM8K at 8B scale, NTP actually beats FSP-RevLM (71.6% vs 70.5%), and the paper frames this as FSP 'narrowing the gap' relative to MTP rather than acknowledging FSP underperforms the simplest baseline on this task.

Standard errors for several comparisons are of a magnitude comparable to reported gains, and no statistical significance testing or discussion of overlapping error bars is provided, making some of the claimed improvements more marginal than the prose suggests.

The paper deliberately restricts MTP and DS-MTP to a single auxiliary head for 'fair' comparison, but this diverges from typical MTP configurations (multiple heads) used in practice/production models like DeepSeek-V3 and Qwen-3, potentially understating what MTP can achieve and thus overstating FSP's relative advantage.

The additional computational cost of training the reverse LM teacher for FSP-RevLM is never quantified; the justification that this cost can be 'amortized' is asserted rather than substantiated with concrete numbers, making it hard to assess true cost-effectiveness versus MTP/DS-MTP.

Pass@k results are reported using the best temperature per method and per task, which risks introducing a favorable evaluation bias for whichever method benefits most from search over temperature, rather than a fixed, pre-registered evaluation protocol.
No code, model, or full dataset release is mentioned, and the proprietary DCLM-like pretraining mixture is not fully specified, limiting reproducibility of the large-scale results.

The synthetic experiments use small GPT-mini models while the main claims are made about 3-8B models; there is no intermediate-scale bridge or ablation demonstrating that the same qualitative mechanisms (shortcut avoidance, adaptive summarization) actually transfer to the large-scale setting beyond aggregate benchmark numbers.

Gains at 8B scale are concentrated on ARC and MATH but are weak or absent on GSM8K, MBPP, and HumanEval+ (ties/near-ties with MTP), so the claimed 'up to 5%' improvement is not representative of overall performance across benchmarks.

strengths: Proposes a well-motivated unified framework (Future Summary Prediction) that cleanly subsumes NTP, MTP, and various recent variants (random-skip, register tokens, DS-MTP), clarifying their trade-offs conceptually.

Strong synthetic diagnostic experiments (path-star graph and modified sibling discovery) that isolate and clearly illustrate the two key claims of the paper: (1) long-horizon summaries help avoid shortcut/teacher-forcing failures, and (2) adaptive/learned summaries are needed when only part of the future is relevant, providing intuitive causal evidence for the design of FSP-RevLM.

Rare-in-the-literature scale of empirical validation: pretraining 3B and 8B parameter models on 250B/1T tokens with six methods compared, which is a substantial and costly undertaking that lends real-world credibility beyond toy tasks.

Reasonably thorough ablations: window length τ, tf-idf reweighting, reverse-model layer depth, pass@k diversity analysis, standard LM metrics (NLL/NTA) as sanity checks, and an additional data-constrained (repeated-epoch) pretraining study showing future-aware objectives are especially beneficial when unique data is limited.
Clear and extensive related-work positioning distinguishing FSP-BoW/FSP-RevLM from SemFormer, ProphetNet, Twin Networks, MiM, BST, and z-forcing.
Preliminary interpretability analysis (attention patterns in RevLM) adds some mechanistic insight into why learned summaries might work.
weaknesses: The headline method (FSP-RevLM) roughly doubles training compute (a same-size reverse model trained for the same number of steps), yet is compared under an ostensibly 'iso-data' framing that downplays this substantial extra cost; the amortization argument for excluding reverse-model training cost is asserted rather than rigorously justified, especially since the reverse LM is a full-scale pretraining run, not a lightweight auxiliary head.

Results are inconsistent across scales: at 3B, DS-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on most benchmarks (MBPP, HumanEval+, ARC-Easy/Challenge), and only at 8B does FSP-RevLM show a clearer overall advantage; with only two scales tested, the claimed favorable scaling trend is suggestive but not strongly established, and could partly reflect scale-specific noise or hyperparameter idiosyncrasies rather than a robust scaling law.
At 8B scale, NTP still wins on GSM8K, undermining the claim of uniform superiority of FSP-RevLM across math/reasoning tasks.

MTP and DS-MTP baselines are deliberately restricted to a single auxiliary head for 'fair comparison,' which, while argued as necessary, also weakens what are otherwise standard multi-head MTP configurations used in practice (e.g., DeepSeek-V3), potentially inflating the apparent gap versus real-world MTP deployments.

Several reported standard errors are exactly 0.000 (e.g., ARC-Easy/Challenge across many methods), which is unusual and raises questions about the evaluation protocol (e.g., near-deterministic greedy decoding) and whether reported small differences are statistically meaningful given only 3 seeds.

Gains, while stated as 'up to 5%,' are often only 1-3 points on many benchmarks, and the paper does not report an aggregate significance test or confidence-adjusted comparison across the many tasks/methods, making it harder to assess whether the overall pattern of improvement is robust versus cherry-picked highlights (e.g., MATH, ARC-Easy at 8B).

No practical solution or analysis is given for the added inference-independent but still substantial training cost of FSP-RevLM; the paper defers 'computationally efficient approaches for learning future summaries' entirely to future work, leaving the core practicality concern of the main contribution unresolved.

The theoretical justification for why FSP reduces teacher forcing/exposure bias remains largely intuitive/qualitative (via the synthetic tasks) rather than a formal or information-theoretic argument, limiting the generalizability of the claimed mechanism beyond the specific synthetic setups shown.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem—limitations of teacher-forced NTP and the short-horizon nature of MTP—and proposes a conceptually clean unifying framework (FSP) that subsumes MTP variants, hand-crafted bag-of-words summaries, and learned reverse-LM summaries.

The synthetic experiments (path-star graph, modified sibling discovery) are well-designed and genuinely illustrative, clearly isolating when long-horizon supervision helps (path-star) versus when adaptive/selective supervision is needed (sibling discovery), and these insights motivate the two FSP variants in a principled way.

Conducting controlled comparisons at both 3B (250B tokens) and 8B (1T tokens) scale, across six objectives (NTP, MTP, DS-MTP, FSP-BoW with different windows, FSP-RevLM), is a substantial engineering effort rarely seen in papers on pretraining-objective research.

The related work section is unusually thorough and carefully differentiates the proposed method from many close prior works (SemFormer, Twin Networks, MiM, BST, z-forcing, ProphetNet), which aids positioning.

The pass@k diversity analysis and data-constrained (iso-compute, repeated-epoch) experiments are interesting additional angles that strengthen the narrative about where future-aware objectives are most useful.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not compute-matched: FSP-RevLM requires training a separate, equally-sized reverse LM, roughly doubling total training FLOPs, yet it is compared directly against NTP/MTP/DS-MTP trained with standard single-pass compute. The paper's justification (treating teacher training as an amortized one-time cost analogous to distillation) is unconvincing in this context, since no such amortization is demonstrated or even attempted, and no control experiment is shown where NTP/MTP are given 2x compute (e.g., more steps, larger model, or ensembling) to check whether the FSP-RevLM gains are simply a compute effect rather than an algorithmic one. This substantially weakens the headline claims.

Results are inconsistent across scale: at 3B, DS-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on 4 of 6 tasks (MBPP, HumanEval+, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge), while at 8B FSP-RevLM wins on most tasks but loses to NTP on GSM8K. This scale-dependent flip-flopping undermines the claim of a 'consistent' improvement and raises concerns about robustness/reproducibility of the method, especially given only 3 seeds and benchmarks known to be noisy (GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, HumanEval+).

Many reported 'gains' are small relative to the standard errors shown (e.g., HumanEval+ FSP-RevLM ties exactly with MTP at 8B; GSM8K differences of ~1 point with overlapping error bars), so it is unclear how many of the claimed improvements are statistically meaningful rather than noise, especially given the benchmark suite is fairly small (6 tasks) and does not include broader standard suites (e.g., MMLU, HellaSwag, BBH).

Despite the introduction's strong motivation around long-horizon planning, narrative coherence, and open-ended creative writing as the core failure modes of NTP/teacher forcing, the empirical evaluation never directly measures long-form generation quality, creativity, or coherence—only math/code/ARC accuracy. This is a significant gap between the stated motivation and the actual evidence provided.

The pass@k evaluation protocol selects, for each method and task, the decoding temperature that yields the highest pass@k from a grid search. This per-method, per-task best-of-grid selection risks inflating and differentially biasing results in favor of whichever method is more sensitive to temperature tuning, and is not standard practice; a single fixed temperature (or temperature selected on a held-out validation split) would be more rigorous.

DS-MTP is artificially restricted to a single auxiliary head to match FSP's single-head design, which deviates from its originally proposed multi-head configuration in DeepSeek-V3; this could handicap a legitimate existing baseline rather than reflecting a fair SOTA comparison.

The novelty of the core learned-summary mechanism (reverse-LM distillation into a forward auxiliary head) is incremental relative to well-known prior work (Twin Networks, Meet-in-the-Middle, Belief State Transformer); the differences highlighted (no parameter sharing, no exact distribution matching, every-position vs. special-token supervision) are reasonable but relatively modest conceptual extensions rather than a fundamentally new idea.

Ablations on summary window length τ, layer depth for RevLM embeddings, and tf-idf reweighting show mixed/inconsistent effects (e.g., no-tf-idf sometimes better), suggesting sensitivity to under-explored hyperparameters without a clear principled recipe, which hurts reproducibility and practical adoption.

strengths: Large-scale pretraining experiments at 3B (250B tokens) and 8B (1T tokens) scale are rare in the literature due to cost, and provide valuable empirical signal beyond typical small-scale ablations.

The paper provides a clean unifying framework (FSP) that subsumes NTP, MTP, and prior future-prediction variants, clarifying conceptual trade-offs (short-range vs long-range, uniform vs adaptive summaries).

Well-designed synthetic diagnostic experiments (path-star graph, modified sibling discovery) isolate the mechanisms behind why MTP fails and why handcrafted vs learned summaries behave differently, providing good intuition before scaling up.
Reasonably thorough ablations at 8B/3B scale comparing MTP, MTP-Skip, FSP-BoW with different window sizes/tf-idf reweighting, and FSP-RevLM with different teacher layers.

Additional data-constrained (multi-epoch) pretraining experiments strengthen the practical motivation and show a consistent trend that future-aware objectives are more useful when unique data is scarce.
Honest discussion of compute trade-offs and extensive, careful positioning relative to a large body of related work (MTP variants, SemFormer, Twin Networks, MiM, BST, etc.).
weaknesses: The main real-world pretraining comparisons (Tables 1 and 2) are not iso-compute: FSP-RevLM requires training a same-size reverse model, roughly doubling total training FLOPs, yet it is compared against NTP/MTP/DS-MTP trained with standard compute. The paper justifies this via a distillation analogy, but no iso-compute baseline (e.g., NTP trained with 2x compute/steps) is shown in the main results, making it hard to attribute gains purely to the objective rather than extra compute.

Results are inconsistent and scale-dependent: at 3B scale, DS-MTP actually beats FSP-RevLM on most benchmarks (ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MBPP, HumanEval+), and the claimed favorable scaling trend rests on a single transition from 3B to 8B, which is weak evidence for a general scaling claim.

Some benchmarks show the proposed method underperforming baselines even at 8B (e.g., NTP beats FSP-RevLM on GSM8K at 8B scale), and FSP-BoW with long windows (τ=100) causes large regressions on ARC tasks (e.g., ARC-Easy drops from 73.6% for MTP to 66.2%), which is not well explained mechanistically.

Given the cost of 8B/1T-token pretraining runs, it's unclear whether the reported 3-seed standard errors reflect independent full pretraining runs or just evaluation-time variability; if the former, the computational claim is impressive but raises reproducibility concerns, and if the latter, the error bars may understate true training variance.

Pass@k evaluation selects the best-performing temperature per method per task, which could introduce a subtle favorable bias for methods whose outputs are more temperature-sensitive, without reporting a temperature-matched or fixed-temperature comparison.

No direct empirical comparison to closely related recently proposed objectives mentioned in text (e.g., Next-latent Prediction, SemFormer, L-MTP) beyond MTP/DS-MTP, despite extensive conceptual discussion of these methods in related work.

The interpretability analysis of the reverse LM's attention patterns is preliminary and largely qualitative/anecdotal (a few cherry-picked heads), offering limited rigorous evidence for the claimed adaptive filtering behavior.
